questions.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-6}^{6}x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g(x)={x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =(-x)^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-g(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $h(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =(-x)^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(-x) \\  & ={x}^{2}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\  & =-h(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Hence, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-1}^{1}{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt[3]{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-4}^{4}x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)={e}^{2x}$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & ={e}^{2(-x)} \\  & ={e}^{-2x} \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is an odd function, but integral II is not of the form ${\int }_{-a}^{a}g(x)\,\text{d}x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. Therefore, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

- The function $h(x)=x{e}^{{x}^{2}}$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =(-x){e}^{(-x)^{2}} \\  & =-x{e}^{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-h(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{4}x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{x}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x=A,$ what is the value of ${\int }_{-5}^{0}\frac{x}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=\frac{x}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\frac{(-x)}{{e}^{(-x)}+{e}^{-(-x)}} \\  & =\frac{(-x)}{{e}^{-x}+{e}^{x}} \\  & =-\frac{x}{{e}^{-x}+{e}^{x}} \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=\frac{x}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}\frac{x}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-5}^{5}\frac{x}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-5}^{0}\frac{x}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{x}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-5}^{0}\frac{x}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x+A & =0 \\ {\int }_{-5}^{0}\frac{x}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x & =-A.\end{aligned}
$$
